question: to the Commission Friedrich Pürner (NI) Subject:
Compatibility of lethal police operations with Article 2 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and investigation transparency standards

The deployment of a special police unit in Berlin (Federal Republic of Germany) resulted in the fatal shooting of a citizen, Abdul B. Article 2 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, read in conjunction with Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), requires Member States to limit any use of lethal force by state bodies to what is strictly necessary and to ensure an effective, independent and transparent investigation. 1.

What legal framework and administrative guidelines exist at EU level to monitor compliance with the principle of proportionality in the context of special police unit operations in the framework of Article 2 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights?

What are the Commission’s minimum requirements for transparency and access to information held by public authorities regarding investigation files (operational protocols, autopsy and ballistic reports) in relation to deaths linked to the use of state force in the Member States?

Does the Commission see a need for reform with regard to uniform standards for independent investigation and public information in the event of the lethal use of firearms by security authorities in the European Union?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.9.2026) Maintenance of law and order is a national competence. However, as the Commission set out in its reply to written question E-004924/20251, any use of force by law enforcement authorities should always be exercised in a proportionate manner. Article 2 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union2 states that everyone has the right to life. However, the Charter applies to Member States only when they are implementing EU law3. It is the responsibility of national authorities and courts to ensure that national measures adhere to fundamental rights as provided for in their constitutional order, and in line with their European and international human rights obligations. In the case referred to by the Honourable Member, it is therefore for the German authorities to conduct independent investigations.
